lead: Tacoma has some of the oldest housing in the Puget Sound area. Long wet winters, century-old basements and aging drain lines make water damage a year-round job here.
risk: old basements, long rainy seasons and aging drain lines
why: More than a quarter of Tacoma homes, 26.9%, were built before 1940. In the North End, Proctor and the Stadium District, many houses have stone or concrete basements that were never meant to stay dry. Months of steady rain soak the ground, and water seeps through foundation walls and floor cracks. Old clay or cast-iron side sewers can crack or fill with roots and back up into the basement.

Rain here is less about one big storm and more about the long season. Wet ground, clogged gutters and downspouts that drain next to the house add up through the winter. Atmospheric rivers can dump inches in a day and push the Puyallup River system high. Damp basements and crawl spaces also stay humid, so mold can start fast if wet materials are not dried.
image_alt: Mold spots on a basement wall after a slow leak in an older Tacoma home
image_caption: Damp Tacoma basements can grow mold if wet materials are not dried quickly.
problems: Older homes with clay or cast-iron lines
tips: Clean gutters each fall and run downspouts well away from the house.
Have an older side sewer scoped with a camera.
Run a dehumidifier in the basement through the wet season.
Store boxes on shelves, not on the basement floor.
areas: Calls come from the North End, Proctor, the Stadium District, Hilltop, Old Town, South Tacoma, the Lincoln District and Fern Hill, plus University Place, Lakewood and Fircrest.

faq.q: Why does my Tacoma basement get wet every winter?
faq.a: Many Tacoma basements are old and not waterproofed. Months of rain saturate the soil, and water pushes through walls and floor cracks. Gutters that overflow and downspouts that drain at the foundation make it worse. Fixing drainage outside often helps more than anything inside.
